Good morning and welcome to, to today's New York City Council hearing for the Committee on Immigration. At this time, I would like to remind everyone to silence all electronic devices. Also, at this point going forward, no one is approaching the dais. No one. Chair, we're ready to begin. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: [GAVEL] I am calling this meeting to order. Good morning, everyone. My name is Council Member Elsie Encarnación, Chair of the Committee on Immigration. Thank you for joining us. Today we will be examining New York City sanctuary protections and the resources available to immigrant communities. It is my pleasure to welcome the new Commissioner of the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs, Faiza Ali. I look forward to hearing your testimony and working with you to strengthen protection for immigrant New Yorkers.

I would also like to thank the representatives from the Administration, members of the public, and my Council colleagues who are here today, including Council Member Alexa Avilés. This hearing is taking place at a time when we are seeing harsh immigration enforcement tactics from the federal government, from arrests of noncitizens attending their required immigration court hearings and ICE check-ins to parents being taken off the streets of our neighborhoods and students from their campus dorms. Donald Trump continues to push a harmful and extreme agenda on cities like New York, but New Yorkers have made it clear they want ICE out of our cities. Across our neighborhoods, people are standing up, organizing protests, sharing Know Your Rights materials, and supporting immigrant-owned businesses. Our communities are doing their part to protect one another and stand against fear and division. In the past, New York City has stepped up to protect immigrant communities in moments like this. In 2017, under the leadership of former Speaker Melissa Mark-Viverito, the Council worked with the

Administration of Mayor Bill de Blasio to strengthen our sanctuary protections. Together, we expanded the role of MOIA, protected immigrant students and consumers, and safeguarded the privacy of all New Yorkers, regardless of immigration status. Because of these laws, the city cannot work with ICE to carry out harmful policies like family separation. New Yorkers need that same leadership again today. This Committee and the Council stand ready to work with MOIA to push back against harmful immigration policies, support our immigrant neighbors, and protect the future of our communities. We look forward to hearing about how our new Mayoral Administration plans to restore MOIA's role as an advisor and convener. This includes helping the city agencies follow our local laws, providing resources to our communities, working with other sanctuary jurisdictions, and advocating for fair and humane immigration policies. New York City must not be complicit in Donald Trump's deportation agenda. Our city has a long history of investing in immigration legal services, Know Your Rights trainings, and language access.

These efforts help ensure that immigrants not only survive in our city, but truly thrive. We look forward to working with the Administration to make sure of that, through both our words and our actions. New York remains a city that protects families, strengthens communities, and stands up for the working people who make this city what it is. Today, the Committee on Immigration will also hear two bills that will strengthen our sanctuary city protections. Introduction 59, sponsored by Council Member Alexa, uh, sorry, 55, sponsored by Council Member Alexa Avilés, will require the Commissioner of MOIA, in consultation with the New York City Law Department, to develop signage that clearly explains key sanctuary protections under local law. The signage would also identify examples of non-public areas on city property and explain the rights people have when interacting with federal immigration authorities. While our nonprofit partners are working hard to hold workshops, inform immigrant communities of their rights, the city must also find ways to share this information more consistently, not only with those

directly impacted, but across all city agencies and staff. I'm very proud to be a co-sponsor on this bill. Introduction 261, sponsored by Council Member Shekar Krishnan, who has joined us as well— hello— would prohibit New York City from entering into contracts with entities that carry out immigration enforcement actions that penalize someone for their presence in, entry into, or reentry into the United States when the city is providing goods or services to those agencies. These bills— these— this bill, excuse me, recognizes the serious harm immigration enforcement can cause to families and communities. It also gives us the opportunity and the responsibility to reevaluate how New York City interacts with ICE in contractual relationships. I am grateful to both Council Member Avilés and Krishnan for introducing these bills and for the continued focus on safety, fairness, and justice for immigrant communities and all New Yorkers. I would like now to thank my Committee Staff for their work in preparing this hearing, including Senate - Senior Legislative Counsel Nicole Catá,

Senior Legislative Policy Analyst Rebecca Barrilla, Principal Financial Analyst Nevdeep Bains, Assistant Finance Director Florentine Kabore. Finally, I would like to thank my staff, Deputy Chief of Staff Stephanie Herrera, Legislative Director Adam Bernstein and Legislative Fellow Winnie Mora, and everybody working behind the scenes to make today's hearing run smoothly, including the amazing Sergeant-at-Arms. Um, did anybody else join us? Nope. Okay, so I would like to now turn it over to Council Member Avilés for brief remarks on her bill. COUNCIL MEMBER AVILÉS: Thank you so much, Chair, and good morning everyone. Um, thank you for being here, uh, for this hearing today, and, uh, Welcome to Commissioner Ali. Um, today we're hearing one of my bills that protects and upholds New Yorkers' rights. Intro 55, the New York City Know Your Rights Act. It makes sure our city workers and residents know their legal rights and responsibilities when it comes to federal immigration enforcement. The bill requires MOIA to create and hang signage on city property telling people about their rights when engaging with federal authorities.

As federal immigration authorities engage in increasingly aggressive and open lawless activity, there should be no ambiguity about our city's sanctuary laws. Clear signage detailing the rights of both employees and individuals in these spaces will give New Yorkers the confidence they need to assert their rights in stressful situations. In the words of, um, a community activist, the signage will purely tell people that you are welcome here, which is an important message to affirm to all immigrants in New York City, regardless of even what it says, which is an important thing for our city. We'll also ensure that our city protects our immigrant neighbors rather than bucking before federal agents' ruses and intimidation tactics. Amid the daily and innumerable horrors coming from this Federal Administration, I'm heartened to see New Yorkers come together to protect one another. Across my district and the city, New Yorkers, including folks in this room, are working tirelessly to lead Know Your Rights trainings, assemble whistle kits, run support hotlines, and do everything they can to protect their people.

It is time for a city to do its part in supporting these grassroots efforts and make sure that everyone entering our city property understands their rights under local laws? Well, one would imagine signage is just a sign, the truth of the matter is we have to do everything in our power to live in and actualize what it means to be a sanctuary, to remind people that sanctuary is not at your discretion or political views. Sanctuary is what our city has leaned into as its own values. And so whether it is signs on every single city property, um, or the assertion by our investment in making sure that people are getting trained and have access. We have to do everything we can to make sure our city is safe. I thank everyone who joined us today to testify and urge my colleagues to support the New York City Know Your Rights Act. Thank you so much. Thank you, Chair. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Thank you, Council Member. I will now turn it over to Council Member Krishnan for brief remarks on his bill.

Thank you so much, Chair Encarnación, for holding today's hearing and, um, my

legislation as well. Good morning, Commissioner. It is good to see you. Good to see you in this role. Um, I'd like to take a moment to discuss my legislation, Intro 261, which is being heard today. Last Thursday, I held my first hearing in the Oversight and Investigations Committee on our city's sanctuary laws and the agency's compliance with them to reaffirm that our city agencies work for us and not for ICE. We are at a perilous moment in our city right now, and right here in New York City. Donald Trump and the federal government are testing the limits of our s— city sanctuary policies. This goes back to last year when we saw the number of instances where the Department of Corrections and the NYPD egregiously violated the sanctuary laws or came very close to doing so. An Administration with Mayor Adams that was eager, sadly, to cooperate with ICE and Borders Are Our Tom Home in any capacity. Our sanctuary laws protect immigrant New Yorkers. They help them feel safe coming to the city government for services, from healthcare to help with housing to care for their children. It's for that reason that city agencies should be working for us,

focusing on the needs of our city, delivering for New Yorkers' needs, and keeping us safe. At a bare minimum, the sanctuary laws make sure that our city government is not cooperating with the enforcement of, uh, federal immigration laws. But even more fundamentally, our sanctuary laws keep New Yorkers safe. They make them feel safe and comfortable coming to city government for the services that they need, not taking on federal immigration responsibilities, not collaborating with ICE, and not increasing the fear that we all feel every day. But our protections against ICE are only as strong as the paper they are— are strong— er, our protections on ICE will only be as strong as the paper they are written on if they are not enforced in reality or strengthened in any way. That's why we are hearing Intro 261 today. It would prohibit New York City from entering into contracts with entities that engage in immigration enforcement and penalize a person's presence in, entry into, or re-entry into the United States. Our city agencies shouldn't be working hand in hand with Donald Trump's deportation agenda, as our Chair so powerfully said. We must do everything we

can to end ICE's presence in our city and make sure that City Hall is working to make New Yorkers' lives safer and more affordable, not increasing fear. Intro 261 would help do that. It would not only f— end future contracts, but end current ones too, allowing us to fully move on from an era under the last Mayoral Administration where we saw egregious collaboration with ICE and Immigration Enforcement. The time is urgent. Thank you so much, Chair. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Thank you. I will now turn it over to the Committee Counsel to administer the oath before we hear testimony from the Mayoral Administration.

Thank you, Chair. We will now hear testimony from the Administration. We will hear from MOIA Commissioner Faiza Ali. Before we begin, I will administer the affirmation. Please raise your right hand. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this Committee, and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
I do.
Thank you. You may begin when ready.

Good morning. Um, thank you to Chair Encarnación and members of the Committee on Immigration for the opportunity to testify today. Um, my name is Faiza Ali, and I'm the new Commissioner for the New York City Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs, or MOIA. By way of introduction, and, um, for some, a reintroduction, I am the proud daughter of immigrants from Azad Kashmir in Pakistan. Growing up in an immigrant household as a woman, as a Muslim, and as a brown New Yorker, shaped my understanding of what my role and responsibility is to the city that I serve. It also shaped how I think about, um, what government should be and the responsibility it carries to serve all communities fairly and remain responsive to their voices. For nearly 20 years, I have worked in community organizing and public service, guided by a simple belief that everyone in the city deserves to be treated with dignity and respect and that government at its best meaningfully, meaningfully can improve the lives of people if it chooses to. I see my role at MOIA a continuation of that work, but this moment requires more than words. It

requires government that is coordinated, that is responsive, and willing to stand clearly on the side of immigrant New Yorkers. At MOIA, our focus is turning values into action. Aligning city agencies to deliver services effectively, strengthening legal protections for immigrant New Yorkers, and ensuring that the city's sanctuary laws are real in people's daily lives. In a time of federal uncertainty, New York City must be a source of stability, dignity, and opportunity for the families who help power this city. As Commissioner, I believe our responsibility is to listen to immigrant communities and ensure that their lived realities shape how government operates. We can build a city where all New Yorkers can lead safe and dignified lives. As federal immigration authorities continue to destabilize and sow fear in our communities, it is important that New York City reaffirms our status as a sanctuary city by living up to our values. That means reaffirming our sanctuary laws not just as policy, but as practice, ensuring that immigrant communities can live, work, and access services and continue to participate in civic life without fear.

All immigrants, regardless of their status, are part of our city. It is our responsibility to ensure that they can build lives of safety and opportunity here. My testimony today will focus on the nature of New York City's sanctuary city laws, the need to ensure its strict adherence to these laws during these times of chaos, and the programs that MOIA operates to support our immigrant communities. First, I want to reaffirm MOIA's fundamental mission to protect all immigrant New Yorkers. The data shows that by ensuring that all New Yorkers regardless of immigration status— can access city services, we can advance public safety and well-being for everyone. Guided by our values and our Charter Mandate, MOIA continues to lead the city's efforts in support of this goal. New York City does not control federal immigration policy, but we can choose whether we let fear guide our daily lives or focus on what we can do to keep New York safe. Under Local Law 228, all city agencies and offices, um, including contractors and vendors, are prohibited from assisting immigration enforcement or utilizing city resources for those purposes, in most

cases. MOIA reports on all requests of, uh, from non-local law enforcement for assistance with immigration enforcement every fiscal quarter, allowing both the public and the City Council to see how the city's sanctuary laws are working and to create an opportunity to address issues or answer questions as needed. Under the leadership of Mayor Mamdani and the issuance of Executive Order 13, the city is committed to review and strengthen implementation of sanctuary laws, including Local Law 228. The executive order requires public safety audits. It creates employee and public education requirements on existing laws, um, and forms an Interagency Response Committee. The public safety audit, which must be completed by early May, ensures that agencies like ACS, DOC, DOHMH, DOP, DSS, and the NYPD are in compliance with the city's laws and requires them to publish their policies and protocols publicly. These agencies are also responsible for training all employees, officers, contractors, and subcontractors. The order also outlines several important roles for MOIA, including coordinating an education campaign about our laws for our colleagues at sister

agencies and the public. We will also work alongside senior Administration leadership on the Interagency Response Committee to provide guidance on preparing and responding to crises. MOIA has already, um, been expanding and sustaining important lines of communication and collaboration with city colleagues. The Interagency Task Force on Immigrant Affairs, uh, meets on a quarterly basis to ensure both ongoing instruction, and communication regarding immigrants' rights issues across city agencies. MOIA's, uh, Communication Campaign is also focused on informing communities of their legal rights under local, state, and federal law, as well as encouraging New Yorkers to call our legal immigration support hotline for immigration help. The campaign is currently, um, hosted in 4,000 Digital Link NYC screens across the city on a 24-hour cycle. Since our last testimony to the Council on sanctuary policies in January 2025, we created several new materials in 10 languages, 10 languages and counting, to respond to some of the immigrant community's most asked questions, including Know Your Rights information available in print and on our

website. Um, today we have our resources available here for the Council and for the members of the public to take with them as well. In 2025, our external affairs team also made more than 35,000 direct touchpoints through resource fairs, Know Your Rights presentations, and canvassing. Over the past 4 years, resources on MOIA's website were also downloaded over 142,000 times by nearly 79,000 users. MOIA is also continuing to work closely with nonprofits to inform immigrant communities of their rights and the availability of city services. Immigrant rights workshops include information about our sanctuary laws, um, our— their rights and protections for immigrant New Yorkers under the New York City Human Rights Law, and how individuals can report violations of their rights. The presentation— the presentations have also served as an additional entry point for community organizations and their clients to connect to free and quality immigration legal services. In FY25, this program delivered 455 presentations that reached nearly 10,000 people, continuing our critical role in outreach to immigrant communities.

And while we cannot control the actions of the federal government, we can and should be proactive in our policies and programs to ensure that fear of enforcement doesn't prevent workers from showing up to their jobs, children from attending school, or families from accessing healthcare and engaging with their broader community. MOIA has also created the necessary legal infrastructure during this time of greatly increased need. Last summer, we launched MOIA's immigration legal support centers, supported by more than $18 million in investments over 3 years to support up to 25 community-rooted organizations providing culturally and linguistically responsive immigration legal assistance. The network currently consists of 35 centers across the 5 boroughs. This model was created to leverage the expertise and experience of nonprofits and community-based organizations that are already embedded in the city's immigrant communities. This initiative provides community members with a variety of legal and non-legal navigation and support services and maintains close outreach and referral partnerships through local schools, hospitals, libraries, houses

of worship, and other local partners, meeting New Yorkers where they are. Since the program's July 2025 launch, the centers have conducted approximately 7,500 comprehensive legal screenings supporting immigrants on a variety of legal needs. All MOIA Centers program providers have free access to select online training and webinars to a nationwide legal technical assistance program through Catholic Legal Immigration Network Incorporated, or CLINIC. The MOIA Legal Technical Mentorship Program provides dedicated support to the LSE network and in FY '26, the immigration— the Immigrant Justice Corps, or the IJC, is offering additional legal technical support for LSEs. Having access to multiple legal technical assistance programs and resources is important for immigration legal professionals to maintain their professional ethical duties, train and support the professional growth of their staff and volunteers, and to advance informed decision-making on advocacy and program out— operations. Providers are also connected to trainings and resources that allow them to respond appropriately to federal policy changes.

Another critical resource available to, um, immigrant communities is Um, MOIA's Immigration Legal Support Hotline, which is also operated by Catholic Charities Community Services and helps New Yorkers explore their options to access comprehensive immigration legal screenings. In calendar year 2025, the hotline received more than 26,000 calls. At the start of 2026, the hotline expanded its service hours to include an additional 3 hours on Monday and Wednesdays from 9:00 a.m. to 8:00 p.m. Um, and New Yorkers can also call the hotline and be connected to services on the last Saturday of each month from 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.. Finally, during this distressing year, MOIA has made substantial use of the Rapid Response Legal Collaborative, or RRLC, which has provided legal assistance to immigrant New Yorkers who are detained or at imminent risk of detention or deportation. Considering the current need, MOIA has increased our investment in rapid response legal, legal efforts by $2 million in this fiscal year. Additionally, MOIA is collaborating with New York City Public Schools Project Open Arms to implement a dedicated referral pathway and Know Your Rights

training for New York City students and their immediate family members who may be eligible for the Rapid Response Legal Collaborative Services. Turning to the legislation before this Committee, MOIA supports Intro— uh, Introduction 55, and we look forward to working with the Council and the sponsor to refine the bill language to reflect the changes recently announced by Mayor Mamdani. And while we have made much progress in the last year, we recognize that there is still much more work to do to protect and support our, our diverse immigrant communities. MOIA stands ready to partner with the City Council, with advocates and community organizations and others to deepen our collaboration and collective impacts in the months and years to come. We're proud that New York City invests more in immigration legal services than any other city in the country and we will continue to explore ways to expand and improve these critical services for our immigrant communities. I thank you and look forward to answering your questions.

CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Thank you so much, Commissioner. Uh, before we go into questions, I wanna, ah, allow the opportunity for our public advocate who has joined us, uh, to say a few words.

Thank you so much, uh, Madam Chair. Brooklyn-born Faiza Ali, it's great to see you over here. Uh, as I mentioned, my name is Jumaane Williams, Public Advocate for the City of New York. I'd like to, uh, thank Chair Encarnación. Did I say it right? CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Almost.

Almost, all right, I'm, I'll try, I’ll keep working on it. My name is Jumaane though, so I understand the feeling. Uh, and the members of the Committee on Immigration for holding this hearing today and for allowing me an opportunity to give an opening statement in the middle of the hearing. Uh, New York City is home to more than 3 million immigrants, and in the- And it is this diverse tapestry of people that makes our city so very special. Right now they are under an unprecedented attack on their civil and human rights, and each of us have a responsibility to protect them.

Similar city sanctuary laws are also under attack. New York City has had laws in place that limit how the city can interact with federal immigration enforcement since 1989, when Executive Order 124 was enacted by then-Mayor Ed Koch. Our sanctuary laws do not shield criminals, they never have, as many claim. In fact, the city allowed to honor detainer requests for individuals convicted of more than 170 different crimes, including rape and murder. Despite all of the fearmongering about sanctuary cities, these laws make us all safer. These protections allow immigrants to report crimes, serve as witnesses, and access schools and city services without fear. These large-scale immigration enforcement operations also divert resources away from initiatives that actually promote safety. It's not just the president leading attacks on our immigrant communities. With the previous Mayor Administration, the call for erosion of immigrant rights came from inside the house as well. Unfortunately, former Mayor Eric Adams issued an executive order to allow ICE to establish an office on Rikers Island and expressed a desire to change the

city's sanctuary laws to allow more collaboration between the city and federal immigration enforcement agencies. Thankfully, our mayor— new Mayor Mamdani feels differently and has issued his own executive order reaffirming the city's immigration protections. Still, we must remain vigilant and thoroughly examine every area that may leave immigrants vulnerable while accessing city services. One area of concern and vulnerability is schools. Schools are not permitted to open their doors to immigration enforcement unless they have a signed judicial warrant. Though we have not seen anyone picked up by immigrant— immigration enforcement either inside K-12 schools or while dropping off their children, we have seen this take place in other localities, and the fear around attending school is real. Students at our colleges and universities, however, have been particularly targeted by this Administration. And just last week, federal agents misrepresenting themselves as NYPD officers took a Columbia student from their dorm and detained her. More importantly, lied about trying to find a young woman who wasn't missing. Thankfully, she has

released— she was released later that day, but the incident exposes concerning vulnerability that requires examination as well as collaboration to ensure it does not happen again. We have also seen immigrants targeted following legal proceedings. When ICE consistently detains people who have lawfully attended an immigration hearing or check-in, it disincentivizes complying with the law and attending these hearings. Federal presence at municipal and state courthouses too can deter people from participating in the legal process, even when they are the one who was victimized or a key witness in a crime. This is why protecting sensitive locations, places like schools, courthouses, hospitals, shelters and places of worship is so important. We must step up where the federal government has stepped back. City agencies are for the people who live and work in New York City, not to serve dubiously legal, dangerous, and wasteful immigration officer enforcement operations. Every person in our city and in our country has inalienable human and civil rights, and we cannot let the humanity— the

inhumanity of this president erode our own humanity. Thank you for giving me the opportunity. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: You are welcome every single time. Um, so first I'd like to say, Commissioner, that I, I am really pleased to hear some of the things that were said during your testimony. Um, I really feel that it, it sounds like we're aligned. And actually, before I keep going, I wanna, um, recognize, uh, Council Member Gale Brewer has joined us. Um, but I do recognize that it seems that we're aligned, right? Uh, you're aligned with the City Charter, advising agencies, best practices for immigrant inclusion, um, compiling quarterly reports and, and things like that. But I want to take a step just to kind of understand the, the world as it stands today. And boy, with MOIA, you're new, I'm new, so I'm kind of gonna get a, a grasp of what's going on there. So currently, how many staffers are on MOIA's staff today?

Yeah, we have a team of about 60 staffers, um, both from that directly come from MOIA and other agency lines.

CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: So 60 staffers that come from other agency lines, but just-
In total. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: In total, and just under MOIA's, uh, staffing lines.

The current direct staffing lines are between 4 and 5. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: 4 and 5, okay and is that the, the total allotted for that? I believe it's, it's more than that, right? It's just what you have hired so far.
Um, that is what is currently allotted. Correct. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Okay and do you have a dedicated staff who advise on the city's detainers?

So we have a pretty robust team currently. We have a, um, a team that does ex— handles external affairs. We have a team that handles policy. Um, we have a legal in, uh, counsel in-house. Um, so we do have the capacity currently to examine whether it's detainer laws, sanctuary laws, um, moving forward. Yes. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: So you will have a dedicated staff member on this team?
Currently have dedicated staff in-house. Yes. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Okay, perfect, thank you. Um, and do— since, and I know you've only been there for a very short amount of time.
This is my day 6. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Day 6, so in the 6 days, um, uh, are there plans, uh, to meet regularly with NYPD, DOC, DOP regarding those detainer requests?

That's an excellent question. So there are 2, um, sort of avenues right now that are before us that, that really, um, dictate our interaction with agencies. So we have first the interagency task force that has existed. It's, it's part of the Charter. It's a Charter mandate. Um, it is where we engage agencies like DOP, DOC, NYPD, but also more broadly other agencies to learn more about any changes to city services that impact immigrant communities. So that is one bucket. Um, and the other is, uh, the Interagency Response Committee that I mentioned in the testimony that comes from Mayor Mamdani's recent executive order that actually, um, si— singles out 6 agencies, including the 3 that you have mentioned, and calls on

them to, um, submit a audit. Um, so we have a better understanding of, uh, how they are adhering to sanctuary policies and laws. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: So in the 6 days that you've been there, have you had any one of these? Have you had an interagency meeting?

I have not in the last 6 days that I've been there, no but we do on the Interagency Task Force, they do meet on a quarterly basis. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Okay. Um, and the Response Committee is still in formation, but, um, uh, I did have a preliminary conversation with a member of the Mayor's Administration on the contours of the, um, Response Committee. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Okay. Um, I am going to now shift gears a little bit, just talking about, um, policy changes. I wanna understand how MOIA's gonna be helping other agencies to prepare to respond to the possibility of ICE agents, uh, waiting to apprehend immigrants at or near hospitals, schools, religious institutions, and shelters?

Mhm. So I, I'll take a, maybe even a further step back just to sort of give a sense of, um, where, what MOIA under the new Administration

will look like and I think that it'll help answer, um, part of your question. Um, it's no secret that under the previous Mayor, um, MOIA was constrained by an Administration that, um, undermined the role of our office. And so we know that that is no longer the case. Um, under Mayor Mamdani, we've, you know, made it very clear that immigration empowerment and, uh, protection is actually a defining commitment of this Administration. So as I assume this role as Commissioner, um, uh, under my leadership, I am looking to lead a more vision-driven approach that really ensures that immigrant New Yorkers are protected, um, that they're heard and that they are in fact able to thrive. So we are looking to build in-house capacity within MOIA centered around a few key, um, areas, protecting immigrants, um, uh, first and foremost, but also looking at how are we advancing affordability and worker protection and how are we increasing the trust, frankly rebuilding the trust between, uh, communities and, and government. So, This is a new MOIA under, um, a, a new Mayor, and we are using this time to really kind of examine,

um, the current program capacities that we have, the current relationships that we have with agencies to really rebuild and strengthen our work. So we're actively looking to ensure that we have the infrastructure to meet, uh, this moment. Um, specifically to your question about how are we preparing for, uh, ICE enforcement activities. And so I've mentioned previously, um, you know, building, uh, MOIA's capacity to, uh, to respond and, and deepen our own rapid response work as one portion. Um, we have capacity right now with our External Affairs Committee that engages the public to make sure that we are meeting the communities where they are. But most importantly, or in addition, um, we are not doing this work in isolation. The Interagency Response Committee is really a, a, a body right now that is looking to develop plans to co— like, for a coordinated citywide response in the event that there is, um, ah, an escalation in federal enforcement. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: And does the in-house capacity also mean hiring more staff or expanding hopefully the budget of MOIA? Do you see the Administration doing that?

So, uh, day 6, I'm still evaluating, um, what our current capacity looks like, um, to make those assessments. And, you know, we have a— another hearing, lucky me, uh, in just a few short weeks to really dig into what the needs are, um, and how we want to build the capacity of MOIA to really meet this moment, um, that, that the communities deserve. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Now, I know in your testimony you mentioned a lot of the Know Your Rights um, both, uh, actual handouts but also trainings that are being done. Is that something that agencies or the public must request through you, and how do they do that? How does someone access the resources that you have? Is it only by the website? Are you proactively looking to reach out to communities?

Yeah, absolutely. That's a great question. Um, there are a number of ways that our Know Your Rights materials are both accessible and, um, available to the public and agencies. So through the Interagency Task Forces, that is where we sh— do a lot of info sharing and material sharing. And so agencies do have access to our most recently updated materials. Um, they are available on our website in multiple languages. We have, um, Know Your Rights

flyers, we have palm cards, we have booklets that really have been updated, um, to reflect what communities are asking for. You know, what, what are the sanctuary laws in New York City? Um, how do they impact New Yorkers? If I am, um, if a family member of mine or someone I know is detained, how do I access services? These are all, um, information that is in— available on our website at nyc.gov/immigrants. Um, and we are, um, also disseminating information through our providers. So we have providers who, um, conduct Know Your Rights trainings, uh, throughout the city in multiple languages. And so we are— they are also carrying that material with them. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: And how often does the MOIA staff, like, go to those, uh, attend those Know Your Rights trainings and, and be present there to give out their own information or interface with, uh, community?

Um, we have staff that, uh, table at, uh, most of these Know Your Rights workshops. We have, um, staff that attend also events that are

unrelated to Know Your Rights workshops that are just in the community. So whether we get a request from an elected official, from members of the Council, or community-based organizations, we do have capacity. We have organizers and, um, and liaisons, community liaisons that actually go out there and table.
